items.title: How to separate human from non-human visits in webserver access logs?
items.summary: I need to perform usage analysis on a few websites based on no more than standard access logs, e.g. Apache's access_log . Entries have a timestamp, a URL path, a client IP address, a HTTP status, and a few more bits, but no USER_AGENT or HTTP_REFERER . Most of the sites are low-volume, so the majority of visits is from bots: crawlers from search engine operators, SEO optimizers, vulnerability scanners, etcetera. Such automated visits must be excluded from the analysis as much as possible. 100% accuracy isn't required, but 90% would be nice. Are any tools or resources available for doing this?

deep.body: I need to perform usage analysis on a few websites based on no more than standard access logs, e.g. Apache's access_log . Entries have a timestamp, a URL path, a client IP address, a HTTP status, and a few more bits, but no USER_AGENT or HTTP_REFERER . Most of the sites are low-volume, so the majority of visits is from bots: crawlers from search engine operators, SEO optimizers, vulnerability scanners, etcetera. Such automated visits must be excluded from the analysis as much as possible. 100% accuracy isn't required, but 90% would be nice. Are any tools or resources available for doing this? E.g. does anyone maintain a public database of IP addresses used by crawlers, that I could use to filter them out by IP address? PS: Linux-based, free solutions are preferred, but I'm interested if there's anything out there that tries to do this.

comments.text: Without the user-agent you can't tell bots apart by name, so you have to combine published IP lists with behaviour in the logs. A workable, free approach: Known crawler IP ranges. Google, Bing and several others publish machine-readable lists, for example Googlebot's googlebot.json and Bing's bingbot.json . Match your log IPs against them (Python's ipaddress module or grepcidr ). For other crawlers, a reverse-DNS lookup of the IP followed by a forward lookup of the returned name is the method Google documents for verifying Googlebot. Datacentre ranges. Humans rarely browse from cloud hosting. AWS publishes ip-ranges.json , and other providers publish similar lists. Dropping hits from those ranges removes most vulnerability scanners and a lot of SEO crawlers.

Isn't it obvious that some nation state or activist/terrorist group has gotten hold of an AI hacking tool/Agent that can wreak havoc? It's not business as usual anymore, it's an agentic cyber war that has started isn't it? * Edit: about bayesian, I wrote two comments below explaining the logic. deep.body: Just looking at history and having some bayesian mindset the fact that: FAA,NSA,MSFT,APPLE,EQUINOR all got hacked in a week. Isn't it obvious that some nation state or activist/terrorist group has gotten hold of an AI hacking tool/Agent that can wreak havoc? It's not business as usual anymore, it's an agentic cyber war that has started isn't it? * Edit: about bayesian, I wrote two comments below explaining the logic. comments.text: Here's my take: Yes, there seems to be a lot of services failing right now. No, I can't see any pattern between these services to conclude a cyber attack. Unless there's some actor that is attacking everything and seeing what sticks, even then, seems unlikely.
What makes you believe such a thing? Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. There is no new cyberwar, if that is what you mean….

Occam’s razor explanation: It's curious that the recent concentrated outages follow the recent adoption of AI by business and software development teams as the way to now do business. Likely causes: 1) existing infrastructure is insufficient to support the speed and volume of AI-generated work, and 2) legacy validation processes applied to AI-generated work can no longer guarantee the quality of output. (Pretty sure that the FAA failure was due to deployment without adequate prior system-level testing; that's not necessarily an AI problem, but AI requires even more rigorous processes than developers are used to these days.) Look in the mirror before advancing conspiracy theories.

> Isn't it obvious that... No. Not in the slightest. Yes, that could that be one possible reason behind it. It would be foolish to deny such a thing. But just because it is possible doesn't make it true. Also consider that if it were all attacks, someone at one of those organizations would have leaked that fact. As that has not occurred, it becomes far more plausible that we are just finally hitting the point where people don't know how their own systems work, and can't fix their problems quickly. Combine that with everyone trying to get the last changes in before the holiday season, and not even knowing those changes in depth, and we get what we are seeing - lots of problems.

It really doesn't matter what people in the affected companies/industries/gov't agencies believe. The important question concerns what the average person on the ground with no insight into any of this believes. Their information sources will be less reliable, more susceptible to manipulation to drive a narrative, etc and they will come from sources that the individual already trusts. I had a relative contact me about steps they should be taking now that Iran, based on a report they caught on their local news, is gonna dirty bomb DC. It's a game of telephone and the American people will not get accurate information from all of their news sources. Many will get information that is intentionally designed to confuse or to drive a narrative. That is what we are up against. Tech industry people should be out front setting the record straight.

Something like the FAA issue could be an example of correlation rather than causation as it pertains to AI. If we take the current explanation as true (that a misconfigured router caused a major network problem) it could still be tied to an over reliance on AI tools. For instance, they may have been relying heavily on such tools to do some of the testing and roll out. Or, they may have been using an AI tool to assist with configurations. It doesn't sound like it was faulty hardware or anything at this point. That reliance may have been what instilled the confidence to make such major changes in the middle of the day.

You're mixing up different events. FAA did not get hacked for example. We still don't know (and probably won't) what happened with NSA. Also it's not "some" actor that got hold of a tool. It's everyone and their dog that got access. If we see thousands of new vulnerabilities announced and patched, you have to expect someone to get lucky, find a different one, and keep it private. > It's not business as usual anymore (...) It's the new normal. It may still get worse before it gets better. Unless the industry as a whole shifts what we're doing, we'll see these kinds of issues for months at least. (Likely years, big systems can't change quickly) By shifts, I mean at the very least taking isolation, sandboxing and verification of basic no-crash properties much more seriously.

items.title: Who's really winning with AI-Coding?
items.summary: I've noticed the same pattern across three different Claude-coded projects now. Initial velocity is strong, but starts to fade until returns are negative. It seems a combination of changes in model behavior and increasing code base size—emphasis on the latter. The larger the code base and documented history/progress (e.g. through updates to completed work and instructions, as in .md files), the more drift starts to set in. At a certain point, you get collapse. This is where it can't maintain consistency within a single unit of work.
